newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian bond yields cut as U.S. takes off.
newsitem.headline: Australian bond yields cut as U.S. takes off.

text.p: *Australian bond yields fell sharply after a strong rally in U.S. Treasuries on Tuesday following weaker than expected data for employment costs and durable goods orders.
*March balance of goods/services due 11.30 a.m. (0130 GMT).
Australian bond yields fell sharply after a strong rally in U.S. Treasuries on Tuesday following weaker than expected economic data.

First quarter U.S. employment costs index rose 0.6 percent when a 0.9 percent rise had been forecast and March durable goods orders fell 3.0 percent, its largest monthly drop since August last year, helping to soothe fears over Fed policy.

"It's just hinting that the Federal Reserve doesn't need to tighten aggressively this cycle, and maybe the near certainty of a May 20 rate hike is becoming less certain," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.

However, there are still several key indicators before the May 20 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, particularly this Friday's April non-farm payrolls report, which if strong could easily see the U.S. rally reversed.

The local market still has to wait until Thursday's average weekly ordinary time earnings and Friday's retail trade data before it can decide its own fate, and whether modest speculation of an easing in monetary policy here gains any momentum before next Tuesday's Reserve Bank board meeting.
Bill futures were also buoyed by the U.S. move with the June contract touching a high of 94.13 in early trading.
This is just below last week's 94.17 peak and equates to a cash rate of 5.87 percent compared with current official interest rates at 6.0 percent.

March balance of goods and services data are due at 11.30 a.m. (0130 GMT) and are forecast to show a surplus of A$150 million after the A$336 million surplus in February, according to a Reuters survey of economist.

However, the market is still familiarising itself with the report, which is only in its third month since replacing the monthly balance of payments report, and is unlikely to have any impact on the market.

Spread differentials to the U.S. widened slightly despite the firm local tone as the market held fire prior to Thursday's domestic wages data. The Canadian market bounced back after its recent underperformance against the bloc, also buoyed by the U.S. data outcomes.
